Flow-priority optimization of additively manufactured variable-TPMS lattice heat exchanger based on macroscopic analysis
abstract: Heat exchangers incorporating triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattice structures have attracted considerable research interest because they promote uniform flow distribution, disrupt boundary layers, and improve convective heat transfer performance. However, from the perspective of forming a macroscopic flow pattern optimized for heat exchange efficiency, a uniform lattice is not necessarily the optimal configuration. This study presented a macroscopic modeling approach for a two-fluid heat exchanger equipped with a TPMS Primitive lattice. Macroscopic flow analysis was conducted based on the Darcy–Forchheimer theory. Under the assumption that heat is transferred solely at the interface between the fluid and TPMS walls, a macroscopic heat transfer model was developed using a volumetric heat-transfer coefficient, which serves as an artificial property characterizing the unit-volume heat transfer capability. To effectively regulate the relative dominance of the hot and cold flows and the channel widths within the heat exchanger, we adopted the isosurface threshold of the TPMS Primitive lattice as the design variable and constructed an optimization scheme for the lattice distribution using a previously described macroscopic model. Optimization was subsequently performed for a planar heat exchanger, where the hot and cold fluids followed U-shaped flow trajectories. The optimal solution was verified, and its validity was examined through detailed geometric analysis and experiments conducted using metal-based laser powder bed fusion. The optimal solution derived from the macroscopic model demonstrated a clear performance improvement over a uniform lattice, with an average enhancement of 24.2% in the detailed-geometry simulations and 23.3% in the experimental results.

title: Advancing multi-material laser powder bed fusion through topology optimized design
abstract: Recent advancements in Multi-Material Laser Powder Bed Fusion (MM-LPBF) offer the unique ability to additively manufacture highly complex structures by selectively depositing multiple material systems within a single layer in the conventional laser powder bed process. MM-LPBF combines the fine resolution of typical LPBF processes with the ability for high resolution spatial control of multiple material placements. The alternating active phase (AAP) algorithm is applied to design a multi-material Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm (MBB) beam, minimizing compliance while also considering manufacturability. Topologically optimized solutions were fabricated through MM-LPBF (316 L stainless steel and CuCrZr) and evaluated through flexural testing with digital image correlation (DIC) and mechanical performance was compared to finite element analysis (FEA). Microstructure characterization of the bi-material interface revealed localized MM-LPBF process-specific defect formation. Mechanical testing revealed progressive stages of failure initiating in the bulk CuCrZr regions and propagating to interfacial regions. DIC analysis indicated that stiffness of the multi-metal MBB structure was within 5.3% of the predicted stiffness from FEA. Findings from this study demonstrate that highly complex multi-material topologically optimized (MM-TO) designs, which were otherwise not plausible to manufacture through either traditional or AM methods, are now feasible at high resolution. The applied method can be extended to other applications which would benefit from multi-objective criterion such as multi-material heat exchangers, biomedical devices, and energy storage devices. Finally, this research highlights the need for further MM-LPBF process development to reduce bulk porosity and interfacial defects, as its processing physics differ significantly from single material LPBF and other metal AM processes.

abstract: Dissimilar sintering trajectories describe temperature- and kinetics-dependent variations in densification behaviors, driven by changes in diffusion mechanisms, phase transformations, and heating rate. Modeling such trajectories is critical for predicting densification and deformation in sinter-based additive manufacturing (AM). This study presents the first investigation of the sintering behavior of 17-4 PH stainless steel produced by paste-based AM process. A modeling workflow based on the continuum theory of sintering is developed, integrating activation energies from mechanistic analysis and accounting for bulk modulus evolution induced by phase transformations. Despite significant variations in sintering trajectory caused by heating rate and decarburization, the model successfully simulates densification during the heating stage, reaching up to 99% density with a root mean square error (RMSE) less than 1.1%. The results provide new insights into the sintering response of paste-based additive manufactured steel and demonstrate the capability of such physics-informed model to capture complex sintering kinetics. The proposed modeling workflow could be generalizable to a wider range of materials exhibiting dissimilar sintering behaviour as well as other sinter-based AM processes.

title: Scan-based fatigue prediction of DED-Arc additively manufactured steel components
abstract: The Directed Energy Deposition process using an electric arc (DED-Arc) enables the manufacturing of customized steel components for civil engineering applications, yet fatigue performance is governed by the characteristic wavy as-built surface resulting from the layer-wise material deposition. Quantifying these notch effects resulting from the surface topography is an essential step for a reliable fatigue analysis of DED-Arc components. In this paper, we present a novel framework for reproducible scan-based fatigue analysis, linking the as-built surface topography to fatigue life prediction without the need for geometric reverse engineering of the 3D-scanned surfaces. To demonstrate its applicability, the workflow is demonstrated on high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel DED-Arc fatigue specimens with distinctive as-built surface topographies, resulting from different DED-Arc printing parameters. Full-field stresses of the 3D-scanned components were computed using the Finite Cell Method (FCM). Local stress concentration factors (SCF) were extracted using multiple variants of the Theory of Critical Distances (TCD) and validated against the results from uniaxial tensile fatigue testing. The volumetric TCD evaluation achieved the highest conformity between the location of the numerical stress concentrations and the experimentally observed fracture locations. Fatigue life was predicted using a local strain model and a regression model with the SCFs resulting from TCD evaluations as scaling factors to the nominal stress ranges from testing. The regression model showed high agreement, with predictions falling within the 3.0 scatter band of the experimental fatigue lives, while the local strain model provided reasonable agreement for fatigue life N < 5 ⋅ 1 0 5 cycles. A more regular as-built surface topography consistently resulted in lower local SCFs and higher fatigue life. The proposed workflow enables reproducible and transferable fatigue life predictions for DED-Arc as-built components across varying surface topographies.

title: Modeling internal reflections of thermal emission in melt pool keyholes to resolve discrepancies in simulated and measured temperatures
abstract: Understanding the formation of defects in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) is important for manufacturing parts that perform to desired specifications. The region of molten material underneath the melting laser beam and inside the vapor depression governs the formation of keyhole porosity in the final part as well as the alloy composition due to preferential evaporation of elements. Although this region is important to defect formation, it is not well quantified by thermal imaging methods because light emitted from a specified region of the surface undergoes reflections in the vapor depression that distort the perceived temperature at the camera. We present a method for simulating thermal imaging experiments on difficult concave melt pool surfaces that accounts for high-temperature reflections, reconciling discrepancies between experimental and simulated thermal fields, and addressing a key challenge in understanding defect formation in Laser powder bed fusion. We begin with bare plate computational fluid dynamics (CFD) temperature profiles and use radiative networks to predict local radiosities that incorporate reflections before passing the light through the simulated optical train to the camera sensor. This process enables an apples-to-apples comparison of CFD predictions of temperature and thermal images. For example, without considering reflections, the maximum deviation in the centerline temperature of 316L steel melt pools is up to 15%. However, with this correction, the maximum deviations are reduced to 4%–6%. Our findings indicate that longer imaging wavelengths reduce the impact of reflections on perceived experimental temperatures. By enabling a more rigorous validation of CFD temperature profiles, the method can help to control for keyhole porosity and powder feedstock alloy composition. Due to the method’s material and surface-agnostic nature, it will also find applications in other fields where understanding high surface temperatures is important such as in aerospace when imaging high-temperature turbine blades, or in renewable energy when working with concentrated solar power technologies.

Ultrafast laser-assisted in-situ hybrid manufacturing: Mechanisms for tailoring processing quality, microstructure evolution and high performance of aluminum alloy

Fibroprinting - hybrid fiber-reinforced (Bio)fabrication via in-situ biomimetic spinning and 3D printing
abstract: One major challenge in the additive manufacturing of soft materials such as thermoplastics, elastomers, and gels is their low mechanical stability. Nature solves this by embedding continuous fibers like collagen or cellulose into soft matrices. Integrating 3D printing into composite materials with fiber spinning has remained difficult due to limited material compatibility, restricted deposition methods, insufficient control over fiber properties, and lack of interlayer reinforcement. We present a spider-inspired technology that combines 3D (bio) printing with in situ biomimetic fiber spinning allowing novel approach for additive manufacturing of fiber-reinforced composites. Fibers with diameter ranging from ca 200 nm to ca 20 μm of microns are drawn from polymer solutions or melts with maximal average speed up to ca 4.4 m/s and deposited via controlled oscillatory motion with placement precision ca 100 μm over distance of at least 10 cm, enabling horizontal or tilted freestanding fibers, precise adjustment of pulling speeds, and fabrication of structures with virtually unlimited thickness. This method surpasses many existing fiber-reinforced additive manufacturing techniques and enables novel complex, fiber-reinforced architectures and composites for biomedical and engineering applications by combining (i) fast deposition of very thin fibers; (ii) their programmed deposition and distribution; (iii) fabrication of free-standing fibers; and (iv) fabrication of samples with virtually unlimited thickness.

Mapping and connecting bulk rheological criteria and microstructure evolution of printable ceramic gels for direct ink writing
abstract: Direct Ink Writing (DIW) is an additive manufacturing technique shifting from lab-based research to industrial-scale manufacturing. DIW offers a clear advantage in materials versatility through formulation design of printable yield stress fluids (YSFs). Quantifying and predicting the printability of YSFs for DIW is an enabling factor for industry adoption. However, commonly reported printability criteria are primarily based on material strength, which cannot capture distinctive rheological features linked to printing behaviour. Other criteria, such as flowability, recoverability, and stretchability, are emerging but are not yet settled in the field. Another critical factor rarely investigated is the YSF microstructure's ability to withstand deformation without disruption.In this work, we use rheo-microscopy to directly map microstructure evolution in pH-responsive strontium titanate (STO) emulsion gels subjected to deformations in shear and extension. Rheo-microscopy, gravity-extension rheology, and direct visualisation during DIW reveal a correlation between microstructure, flow instabilities, and printability. Here we demonstrate that complementary bulk rheological measures in shear and extensional flows and microstructure evolution are all key factors to understand and quantify rheological printability criteria in DIW.

title: Tailoring phase transformation temperatures and functional properties through laser-based powder bed fusion: A pathway to functionally graded NiTi shape memory alloys
Mechanistic understanding of powder capture in simultaneous wire–powder direct energy deposition of metal matrix composites
Creep property of Ni-based superalloy fabricated by laser-wire-based DED forming dot-shaped beads
abstract: The laser-wire-based directed energy deposition (LW-DED) is an additive manufacturing (AM) process that achieves high material utilization and high-quality parts and is suitable for large-part manufacturing and repair applications. In this work, we mainly investigated the creep behavior and influencing factors of Inconel 718 deposited by LW-DED forming dot-shaped beads, which is expected to be advantageous in reducing residual stress by suppressing heat accumulation. The deposited material was heat-treated with a homogenization treatment at 1050 °C to dissolve detrimental phases such as Laves phases and δ phases. Subsequently, it underwent a standard aging treatment. The creep properties of the deposited material had anisotropy. The deposited sample prepared with its loading direction perpendicular to the building direction exhibited a creep lifetime approximately 1.7 times and 1.4 times that of the deposited sample prepared with its loading direction parallel to the building direction and the commercial wrought Inconel 718, respectively. It was estimated that the microstructure, which has the <001> crystallographic orientation parallel to the building direction, leading to higher Taylor factor, as well as its γ” precipitates that grows coarsely during the creep, its low dislocation density and large-sized grain, is the factor that realizes superior creep properties. Thus, the usefulness of Inconel 718 manufactured by using LW-DED, which forming dot-shaped beads, was demonstrated.

title: Material extrusion additive manufacturing of high iron particle loaded polymer filaments for axial flux motor stator
Influence of printing parameters on geometric and topological evolution of intra-filament voids in 3D printed concrete
abstract: Assessing the long-term durability of extrusion-based 3D concrete printing is becoming increasingly important due to the expansion of its application to real-scale construction. Many studies have focused on the bonding properties of the layer interface, resulting in improvements of interface quality. However, the manufacturing process introduces unique intra-filament voids within the filament which potentially influence the durability of 3D printed concrete. Despite the irregular geometry of intra-filament voids depending on the process, the effects of printing parameters on the intra-filament void structure have been limitedly evaluated. Most studies have restricted the observations to a single printing condition and have not investigated the relationship between the manufacturing process and intra-filament void evolution. This study investigated the geometric and topological evolution of intra-filament voids under three printing conditions, such as layer pressing, over-extrusion and no-pressing. We employed X-ray computed tomography to quantify the intra-filament void structures. Geometric analysis based on solidity and sphericity revealed that the printable mixture with superplasticizer (SP) demonstrates multiple voids coalescence. On the other hand, the mixture without SP exhibits individual void deformation, such as flattening and elongation. Furthermore, we conducted the recently developed topological data analysis technique, persistent homology (PH). The PH analysis characterised the topological evolution of intra-filament voids, and the principal component analysis of the resulting persistent diagrams demonstrated that the layer pressing condition showed consistent topological void structures. This geometric and topological approach might provide a new descriptor to correlate the process-induced intra-filament voids and the properties of printed objects.

title: Revealing optimal melting regimes for defect lean single-track aluminium laser powder bed fusion builds
abstract: AlSi10Mg is a typical alloy used in additively manufactured components such as heat exchangers with thin-wall features. However, printing of single-track thin walls remains a challenge owing to inherent process instabilities. Here, we use in situ synchrotron X-ray imaging to develop a process map identifying five distinct melting regimes with their characteristic defect formation tendencies. Quantification of melt pool shape, void formation and melting efficiency, point to an optimal, defect-lean keyhole regime for single track builds with a high melting efficiency of 25% and an energy reduction of ~30% from the commonly used conduction regime. The unstable keyhole region was found to be larger than that reported for other alloys, e.g. Ti-6Al-4V. We also reveal a transitional keyhole flickering phenomenon, causing irregular tracks due to rapid (~1 ms) switching between keyhole and conduction modes, which is explained with the aid numerical simulation and correlated with melt pool size, physical properties and the dimensionless Strouhal number. Process mapping enhances our understanding of processing strategies for thin-wall builds, informing robust, high-quality additive manufacturing methods.

title: New mechanistic insights of dislocation configurations in strain hardening of additively manufactured 316 L stainless steel
Beyond the material-per-function paradigm: Functionally graded active structures via laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing of nickel- titanium shape memory alloys
Excellent strength and ductility synergy of a new LPBF-manufactured HSS via sequential activation of multiple deformation mechanisms
Limitations of grain refinement in solute-modified CoCrNi: The role of constitutional supercooling in PBF-LB
abstract: Additive manufacturing of medium-entropy alloys offers unique opportunities for fabricating complex metallic components with enhanced mechanical properties. However, this processing route is often challenged by microstructural anisotropy and the formation of columnar grains. In this study, a solute-based strategy leveraging constitutional supercooling was explored to promote grain refinement in a CoCrNi alloy. Ti was selected through thermodynamic calculations due to its high growth restriction factor ( Q ) and favorable solubility, and a (CoCrNi) 97 Ti 3 (at%) composition was produced via in-situ alloying using powder bed fusion - laser beam. Although grain size refinement was not observed, Ti addition disrupted columnar grain growth and promoted a more equiaxed morphology, likely due to modified melt pool dynamics associated with in-situ alloying. Complementary casting and single-track experiments confirmed that steep thermal gradients inherent to PBF-LB processing can suppress solute-driven grain refinement. Thermal analysis further revealed lower experimental Q values compared to predictions, evidencing limitations in the thermodynamic data employed. Additionally, the high solidification rates during laser processing slightly reduced segregation, contributing to a slightly lower effective Q value. These findings highlight the importance of linking solute selection with process-specific solidification conditions and provide new insights into the combined effects of alloy chemistry, melt pool dynamics, and thermal gradients in medium-entropy alloys processed by additive manufacturing.

title: Process-agnostic multi-metric nondestructive characterization of porosity in additive manufacturing via specialized single-camera two-wavelength pyrometry
abstract: Predicting and quantifying pores in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) remains limited by models tailored to narrow process regimes and by conventional thermal sensing that is highly sensitive to emissivity, both of which fail under realistic process variability. Here, we introduce a process-agnostic, context-aware deep learning framework for quantitative, multi-metric pore characterization, enabled by our patented single-camera two-wavelength imaging pyrometry (STWIP) system. This novel high-speed (up to 100,000 frames per second (fps), with 22,500 fps demonstrated in the present study), high-resolution diagnostic uniquely captures spatiotemporal melt pool thermodynamics and morphology with physical fidelity, overcoming emissivity and alignment challenges inherent to conventional monitoring. By integrating frequency-domain and temporal representations across adjacent layers and laser scans, the optimized model achieves 88% accuracy, 85% precision, and 84% recall for pore-presence detection, with 83% mean accuracy for pore count and size and 72% for porosity ratio across unseen test sets. Performance remains robust, albeit slightly lower, on entirely new builds. These results are remarkably strong given the numerically small ground-truth pore metrics and the extreme data imbalance and process variability of realistic LPBF, and they substantially exceed prior qualitative or regime-specific approaches. Our method enables robust, quantitative, and potentially transferable defect prediction across regimes, advancing real-time quality assurance in metal additive manufacturing.

title: Microstructural screening of intermetallic alloys via an additively manufactured L12-Ni3(Al,Ti)/L12-Co3(Al,W) diffusion couple
Large-scale multi-particle cold spray simulation framework for deposit morphology and deformation analysis
abstract: Cold spray (CS) is a solid-state particle deposition technology extensively utilized for coating and more recently for additive manufacturing applications. While detailed numerical modeling of CS deposition offers substantial benefits for process optimization, existing methods are hindered by significant computational demands. As a result, simulations are typically confined to a small number of powder particles, which does not adequately reflect the actual deposition dynamics and therefore limits the effectiveness of simulations for deposition assessment. In this study, a high-fidelity open-source multi-particle impact framework (Free2Spray) is developed to simulate large-scale (>10,000 particles) CS deposition at a considerably convenient computational cost. The model can accurately track material changes during deposition by splitting the process into sections, each with randomly placed particles. These sections are added step by step, carrying over all data from one to the next. Python scripts are developed to automate this workflow, requiring the user to specify a few key parameters. The framework is also equipped with our recently developed high-precision material model implemented via a user-defined hardening (VUHARD) subroutine to accurately capture the realistic particle deformation. The developed framework is proven to accurately predict the shape profiles and surface roughness of experimental single-layer single-track deposits under various nozzle scanning speeds and reproduces the experimental cross-sectional particle deformation and flattening ratios. Compared with the standard Eulerian schemes, the proposed framework reduces the computational time and memory usage by 34% and 35%, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly improves computational efficiency while maintaining high accuracy, enabling personal computers to simulate the CS deposition process with ten million elements and providing a reliable tool for predicting deposit morphology and particle deformation behavior. The source codes are provided ( https://github.com/xuanyge/Free2Spray.git ) to enable interested researchers to utilize and implement them.

title: Combined thermal and illuminated imaging for cooling rate measurements in laser powder bed fusion
abstract: In this work, we present a technique for simultaneous ratiometric (two color) and illuminated imaging of the laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) process using a single RGB color camera and a blue laser illumination source. Thermal data are collected via ratiometric temperature measurement and morphological data such as melt pool length and width are segmented from illuminated image frames with the assistance of a UNet machine learning model. By tracking the evolution of these features over time and combining them to calculate temperature gradients, we demonstrate the feasibility of accurately estimating solidification cooling rates in the tail of the melt pool directly from RGB video data. Travel direction cooling rates in 316L stainless steel melt pools are measured to be between 1.7 × 1 0 5 and 3.0 × 1 0 6 K/s and show an inverse relationship with increasing melt pool linear energy density. Cell spacing measurements from single tracks and cooling rate vary as a power law correlation with an R 2 value of 0.958. Reasonably high correlations (R 2 value of 0.72-0.84) are seen between cooling rates and individual camera channel signals, paving the way for part-scale cooling rate monitoring.

title: Effect of fabrication restrictions on topology optimized 3D printed concrete structures
abstract: Concrete 3D printing (3DPC) has the potential to eliminate formwork and reduce material consumption in the construction of geometrically complex, non-repetitive structures. However, fully leveraging these advantages requires design methodologies that reflect the strict fabrication constraints inherent to 3DPC. This paper introduces a mixedinteger nonlinear programming (MINLP) topology optimization framework for truss-like 3DPC structures that directly incorporates major fabrication constraints and characteristics: discrete and/or manufacturable member dimensions, machine-specific minimum turning radii, toolpath continuity, and displacement and stress limits for brittle, plain concrete. The design method is demonstrated on a 2.5D bridge design and validated through fabrication and experimental testing of a 2.3 m specimen. The performance of the as-printed structure agrees with numerical predictions and highlights the feasibility of producing fully printable, fabrication-aware, optimized designs without extensive postprocessing. A complementary numerical study quantifies the influence of individual manufacturability constraints, revealing that the current limitations in 3DPC hardware drive resulting material usage in optimal designs. The fabricated design offers 14% material savings compared to a conventional cast alternative, but this can be increased significantly with relatively small improvements in 3DPC technology. The most pronounced effect is the reduction in discrete deposition width, which can achieve a 99.8% weight reduction compared to a cast design. Another, more technologically challenging way to increase material savings from 14% to 28.6% is to eliminate the continuous toolpath requirement. The smallest observed effect is associated with decreasing the turning radius.

title: Multi-phase semi-resolved CFD-DEM for high-fidelity modeling of powder-based directed energy deposition
Rethinking the role of flow resistance in fibre breakage during material extrusion of discontinuous recycled carbon fibre reinforced thermoplastic composites
abstract: This study develops an efficient coupled computational fluid dynamics and discrete element method (CFD-DEM) model to investigate the breakage mechanisms of long discontinuous fibres during material extrusion additive manufacturing. Simulations were conducted with different fibre length distributions to explore fibre breakage behaviour and its relationship with flow resistance evolution. The results indicate that fibre structures with higher flow resistance tend to generate stronger local stress concentrations, leading to increased fibre breakage. To further investigate the role of flow resistance, planar shear simulations are performed to identify fibre structures with reduced resistance. These structures were subsequently examined under extrusion and deposition conditions. The simulations show that introducing short discontinuous fibres can initially reduce macroscopic flow resistance and delay early stage breakage. However, under the investigated conditions, the resulting evolution of fibre interactions and local stress localisation can ultimately lead to greater overall fibre breakage. The findings highlight the coupled relationship between fibre length distribution, flow resistance, local stress evolution and fibre breakage under the investigated CFD-DEM conditions. More broadly, this study provides simulation supported mechanistic insight into how fibre length dependent structural evolution influences breakage behaviour during extrusion and deposition.

title: Compositional modulation enables crack suppression through grain refinement in laser powder bed fusion W-Nb
Achieving high strength and corrosion resistance of Al/Cu bimetals via blue-laser directed energy deposition additive manufacturing
Subtractive composition design of nickel-aluminum bronze for laser additive manufacturing: Achieving superior as-deposited mechanical and corrosion performance
Enabling interlocking joint design for multi-material additive manufacturing via topology optimization with discontinuous interfacial property
abstract: Multi-material additive manufacturing (MMAM) offers the potential to create functionally graded structures with tailored properties; however, its structural integrity is often compromised by weak bonding at material interfaces, which leads to premature delamination or structural failure. To address this challenge, geometric interlocking has been identified as the optimal reinforcement strategy for connections characterized by weak interfaces; however, existing approaches rely on human intuition to design interlocking geometry. This work proposes a multi-material topology optimization method to autonomously generate such interlocking features by explicitly modeling the interfacial weakness. Specifically, the method utilizes a Heaviside-based interpolation to model the material interface as a discrete region with reduced elastic modulus. This formulation compels the optimizer to evolve from a standard flat boundary between two materials into a stair-stepped, interlocking joint in order to maximize overall stiffness of the structure. Comparative analysis demonstrates that while standard continuous interpolation results in simple planar interfaces, the proposed Heaviside-based interpolation method successfully drives the formation of discrete geometric locks autonomously. The performance of the optimized structure is shown to outperform a robust human-designed interlocking joint through MMAM and tensile testing. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach offers a simple yet effective solution for enhancing the interfacial strength and reliability of multi-material additively manufactured components.

title: Material-agnostic temperature field prediction for metal additive manufacturing via a parametric PINN framework
abstract: Accurate temperature field prediction in metal additive manufacturing (AM) is essential for understanding the process–structure–performance relationship. While prior studies have explored generalization to unseen process conditions, they often require extensive datasets, costly retraining, or pre-training. Generalization across different materials also remains relatively unexplored due to the challenges posed by distinct material-dependent thermal behaviors. This paper introduces a parametric physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework for generalization across unseen materials without labeled data, retraining, or pre-training. The framework adopts a decoupled parametric PINN architecture that separately encodes material properties and spatiotemporal coordinates, fusing them through conditional modulation to better align with the multiplicative role of material parameters in the governing equation and boundary conditions. Physics-guided output scaling derived from Rosenthal’s analytical solution and a hybrid optimization strategy are further incorporated to enhance physical consistency, training stability, and convergence. Experiments with numerical simulations across diverse metal alloys, including both in-distribution and out-of-distribution cases, demonstrate effective generalizability along with superior training efficiency. Specifically, the proposed framework achieved up to a 64.2% reduction in relative L 2 error compared to the non-parametric baseline while surpassing its performance within only 4.4% of the baseline training epochs. Ablation studies clarify each component’s contribution and scrutinize the severe training instability prevalent in conventional parametric PINNs. Overall, the proposed framework provides an efficient and scalable material-agnostic solution for temperature field modeling, contributing to more flexible and practical deployment in metal AM.

title: Oscillating laser directed energy deposition for manufacturing high-performance titanium alloy
Rheological insights into vat photopolymerization 3D printing of colloidal suspensions
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates how shear thinning and thixotropic recovery govern the vat photopolymerization (VPP) processing of high-viscosity fumed silica (FS)-filled colloidal photopolymer resins. Hydrophobic FS (Aerosil R972) was incorporated into a commercial acrylate resin to create suspensions with tunable viscosity, yield stress, and recovery behavior. Rheological measurements showed that FS loading induces strong non-Newtonian behavior, with reversible network breakdown under shear and time-dependent structural recovery after shear cessation. Photo-rheology indicated that FS loading up to 10 wt% did not significantly alter bulk curing kinetics under the tested conditions, while ultra small angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) confirmed post-shear particle re-agglomeration and network rebuilding. Printing experiments demonstrated that shear thinning enables processing of the 4 wt% FS formulation despite its zero-shear viscosity exceeding the commonly cited VPP limits. However, the 8 wt% FS resin exhibited defects, including bottom-layer overgrowth, layer thinning, and slanting, highlighting the narrow processing window for highly filled thixotropic systems. Mechanical testing of green-state specimens revealed a slight tensile reinforcement from R972 FS. Interlayer wait time showed a stronger influence on layer morphology, dimensional accuracy, and mechanical properties than build-head speed within the tested conditions and samples, where a wait time of 60 seconds provides necessary thixotropic recovery at the cost of ultimate mechanical strength. While SEM of the printed samples showed subtle differences in morphology under different wait times, the study revealed that more complex flow and recovery processes exist beyond the rheological preview. Overall, this work establishes how a rheology-guided framework can support our understanding and processing of high-viscosity colloidal resins in VPP.

title: A conversion-driven optical framework for penetration depth and lateral overcuring in ceramic vat photopolymerization
Physics-based acoustic monitoring of keyhole regime transitions in laser powder bed fusion validated by operando synchrotron X-ray imaging
abstract: Additive manufacturing by Powder Bed Fusion using a Laser Beam on Metals (PBF-LB/M) enables unprecedented design freedom but remains limited by defect formation that stems from unstable melt pool dynamics. Current monitoring approaches often depend on machine learning, which can obscure the underlying physics and complicate industrial deployment. Here, a direct acoustic emission-based methodology is introduced that captures sound signatures of conduction-keyhole transitions and keyhole collapse. Using acoustic emission measurements validated by operando synchrotron X-ray imaging, a series of envelope-based indicators are established that robustly distinguish stable and unstable regimes in 316L steel and Ti6Al4V under continuous and pulsed lasers. This physics-driven framework provides transparent, localized regime prediction, paving the way for more reliable and industrially scalable monitoring solutions in metal additive manufacturing.

title: A fluid-dynamics-based analysis of droplet coalescence in Arburg Plastic Freeforming: A case study with polycarbonate
Machine learning–aided in-situ ultrasonic characterization for multi-parametric monitoring of vat photopolymerization
abstract: Comprehensive, real-time characterization of curing evolution remains a critical challenge for ensuring the geometrical accuracy and mechanical integrity of vat photopolymerization (VPP). Here, we present a physics-informed, machine-learning-enhanced in-situ ultrasonic monitoring (IUM) framework that simultaneously estimates three key in-process part properties—degree of conversion (DoC), storage modulus, and final thickness—during digital light processing VPP. A 10 MHz pulse-echo transducer integrated into the printhead acquires six ultrasonic waveforms at each printed layer. Guided by ultrasonic wave-propagation physics, the measured signals are transformed into complementary layer-wise, part-scale, and printing-condition descriptors that jointly capture the coupled evolution of propagation path length, elastic stiffening, and viscoelastic attenuation during curing. These multimodal inputs are fused through a lightweight attention-based deep neural network. Comparative evaluation under a leak-free Leave-One-Intensity-Out (LOIO) cross-validation protocol identified a three-branch architecture excluding raw waveforms as the optimal configuration. Across five random seeds and ten LOIO folds on 50 printed samples, the deployed model achieved RMSEs of 0.094 ± 0.008 mm for thickness (R² = 0.985), 8.60 ± 0.07 kPa for storage modulus (R² = 0.832), and 0.014 ± 0.001 for DoC (WMAPE = 1.50%, R² = 0.757). Attention analysis showed that IUM-derived features accounted for approximately 57% of the fusion-layer contribution, demonstrating that in-situ ultrasonic sensing provides information beyond nominal printing conditions. Feature attribution further revealed physically consistent relationships between ultrasonic signatures and material evolution, with thickness governed primarily by propagation-path growth, storage modulus by frequency-domain descriptors associated with acoustic dispersion, and DoC by within-layer curing dynamics coupled with exposure intensity. The deployed model performs inference in 2.3–4.7 ms per layer, enabling real-time implementation. By integrating ultrasonic wave-propagation physics with multimodal learning, this framework provides a practical pathway toward adaptive process control and autonomous, defect-free photopolymer additive manufacturing.

title: Key process variable tolerances and their impact on the tensile and fatigue performance of additively manufactured Ti-6Al-4V
A design-to-manufacturing framework for graded woodpile structures via programmable dual-resolution material extrusion
Strength and ductility of an in-situ alloyed additively manufactured titanium alloy with composition-induced microstructural heterogeneity
Printing fidelity improvement during immersion-phase-separation-based embedded printing of polymers
Deposition dynamics mechanism and prediction model of electric-field-driven jets on liquid film substrate
Influence of thermal conductivity on the productivity of Al alloys designed for LB-PBF
abstract: One of the main limitations of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is its limited productivity, which directly impacts the cost of fabricated components. Here, we investigate how tailoring the thermal conductivity of aluminium alloys can enhance productivity. Several alloys were designed by varying transition element concentrations (Mn, Cr, and V) to decrease thermal conductivity. Lower thermal conductivity results in larger melt pools by reducing heat dissipation through the substrate. These enlarged melt pools enable the use of larger hatch spacings and thicker powder layers while maintaining sufficient overlap between adjacent tracks and preventing lack-of-fusion defects. The build rate of one of the least conductive alloys, Al-0.5Fe-1.2Zr-2Cr (wt%), reaches 63.5 cm³ /h while maintaining a pore volume fraction below 0.5%. This represents a substantial improvement compared with typical build rates reported for AlSi10Mg (20–25 cm³/h), demonstrating that low thermal conductivity alloys offer an extended processing window towards higher productivity. The microstructure of a novel Al-0.5Fe-2Cr-1.2Zr (wt%) alloy, among the least thermally conductive compositions investigated, was characterized in the as-printed condition. EBSD revealed a bimodal grain structure, with fine grains located at melt pool boundaries and coarse columnar grains within melt pool interiors. Coarse faceted Cr-rich precipitates were observed in the fine-grained regions, whereas globular Fe-rich eutectic dispersoids formed within melt pool interiors. Atom probe tomography revealed a highly supersaturated Al matrix, particularly enriched in Cr, intentionally added to reduce thermal conductivity. These extended supersaturations result from out-of-equilibrium solidification conditions and provide opportunities for designing high-productivity aluminium alloys for LPBF.

Temperature control of digital glass forming processes
Nanosecond laser-induced forward transfer for single metal microdroplet printing: Interfacial engineering via transition layers
Distortion-minimized de-homogenization for optimization of cell-size distribution in TPMS structures
abstract: This paper presents a homogenized topology optimization (TO) method for spatially optimizing cell-size distribution of triply-periodic minimal surface (TPMS) structures, with high accuracy in the optimized structural response after de-homogenization. To achieve this, we introduce a novel de-homogenization technique that directly minimizes the difference between the wavenumbers obtained from the target and actual size distributions. This minimization problem is efficiently solved as a typical Poisson’s equation utilizing the discrete cosine transform (DCT). We first verify the proposed de-homogenization method through numerical examples, showcasing its capability in significantly reducing the known distortion of the de-homogenized TPMS structures from the conventional periodic modulation (PM) method. Then, we apply the proposed method to a stiffness maximization problem, to demonstrate its effectiveness in improving the structural response compared to the PM method, through numerical examples and experimental validation. The proposed method successfully reduced the distortion of the de-homogenized structures compared to the PM method, leading to 0.8% difference in the strain energy compared to the homogenized model, as opposed to 63.6% difference in the PM method. The optimized structure from the proposed method shows a significant improvement in the strain energy by 50.1% compared to the uniform case in the FE analysis on the de-homogenized models, while the PM method results in a significant decrease of 45.8%. The experimental validation shows that the effective stiffness of the optimized structure from the proposed method is 54.2% higher than that of the uniform case, while the PM method results in a significant decrease by 77.3%. These results exhibit the proposed method effectively increases the accuracy of the de-homogenization, thereby maximizing the potential of the homogenized TO for the spatial cell-size optimization of TPMS structures.

title: 3D semi-analytical thermo-elasto-plastic model for additive manufacturing
abstract: In additive manufacturing (AM), stress field drives defects like distortion, warping, and promoting delamination and cracking. Fast, accurate stress prediction is therefore essential for AM process planning and control, including real-time adaptive control, AM digital twins, data-driven and physics-driven workflows. However, spot-wise thermo-elasto-plastic finite element method (FEM) are often too slow for design iteration or real time use. Existing semi-analytical thermo-elasto-plastic approaches achieve high speed but are largely limited to 2D. In this paper, a full 3D semi-analytical thermo-elasto-plastic model for AM is built. The method uses a spot-wise analytical thermal field as the load and computes displacements and stresses via Green’s function representations on a half space, with plastic flow integrated by an implicit return-mapping algorithm. A surface consistent singular integral regularization at the traction free top surface ensures stable, accurate evaluation of displacements and stresses when sources lie on or near the surface. The proposed model is validated against FEM for transient temperature fields, thermo-elastic responses, thermo-elasto-plastic stress and displacement fields, and residual stresses after cooling. Under temperature-independent material assumptions, the semi-analytical solution closely matches FEM for single-track and multi-track cases. For comparison with an FEM model using temperature-dependent material properties, the semi-analytical thermal solution reproduces the FEM temperature field when constant thermal properties are selected near 650 °C, and stress agreement improves when the temperature-dependent yield strength is updated during return mapping. The residual stress comparison shows that the model captures the dominant longitudinal residual stress and von Mises residual stress after cooling. Runtime comparisons indicate up to 1,670× speedup compared with FEM on consumer-grade hardware. The method’s speed enables scalable data generation, adaptive control and optimization-oriented AM process modeling.

title: Stepwise martensitic transformation in tool steel during laser powder bed fusion revealed by operando X-ray diffraction
abstract: A mechanistic understanding of phase transformation behaviour under extreme thermal conditions is essential for controlling microstructure and performance of additively manufactured metallic components. However, direct experimental evidence capturing phase evolution during rapid solidification remains limited. In this study, phase transformations in M50 tool steel processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) were investigated using operando X-ray diffraction in reflection mode to monitor phase evolution during laser melting and subsequent cooling processes. Under cooling rates in the order of 10 5 ℃/s, austenite formed directly from the liquid while δ-ferrite formation was suppressed. Martensitic transformation proceeded in a stepwise manner, with significant changes in phase fraction occurring at different cooling stages, highlighting the influence of rapid solidification on martensite nucleation and growth. Distinct transformation stages were identified, consisting of early abrupt transformation stages followed by later stages characterised by more gradual transformation. The carbon content in martensite increased from 0.58±0.04 wt.%to 0.68±0.02 wt.%, as determined from the evolution of local tetragonality. While variations in LPBF volume energy density had a limited effect on the cooling rate, lower energy densities were associated with higher martensite tetragonality and carbon enrichment. These findings provide valuable insights into phase evolution in rapid solidification processes for tailoring microstructure through manufacturing process control in additively manufactured steels.

Design for tape-reinforced additive manufacturing using geometric projection topology optimization
abstract: The pursuit of high-performance structures requires innovative manufacturing approaches that balance multiple competing factors. This work focuses on one such novel approach, named Advanced Tape Laying Additive Manufacturing (ATLAM), that integrates the characteristics of automated tape laying and additive manufacturing. ATLAM supported by a dedicated complementary design tool can provide a unique ability to balances mechanical performance, manufacturing flexibility, and eco-efficiency. To exploit the full potential of ATLAM in manufacturing lightweight sustainable structures, we aim to develop, verify and experimentally validate a computational design tool rooted in topology optimization. We use geometric projection topology optimization framework, and tailor it to accommodate ATLAM’s unique features and constraints. We customize the geometric primitive, the projection & material interpolation schemes and design/manufacturing constraints. Then, based on numerical investigation, we showcase excellent effectiveness and robustness of the proposed approach in optimizing geometry and reinforcement placements and designing stiffer yet manufacturable structures. An environmental impact constraint is incorporated to enable a design choice on sustainability. Finally, we experimentally validate our proposed approach, paving the way for reliable use in real-world applications.

Reduction of baseplate distortion during directed energy deposition using compliant features
abstract: Distortion in additive manufacturing (AM) remains a barrier to its adoption in precision industries. Baseplate warpage is one such issue which compromises the feasibility of post-process precision machining. The restriction to thermal contraction of the deposited part, imposed by the baseplate, generates bending moments that, in turn, causes warpage. A novel distortion mitigation strategy using baseplates with integrated compliant features, which enables thermal contraction of the build is presented. Six unique design concepts, including a solid reference, are evaluated using two deposition geometries. A laser, hot-wire, directed energy deposition (DED) process is used to deposit a symmetric cylindrical part (C-part) and a T-shaped asymmetric part (T-part). Flatness deviation of baseplates is measured using structured light 3D scanning. Measurements reveal a reduction in net flatness deviation of 58.8% for the C-part and 40.9% for the T-part, compared to the solid reference. While most designs yielded reductions exceeding 30% and 20% for the C- and T-parts, respectively, one configuration resulted in increased deviation. Finite element (FE) simulations are performed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms affecting distortion of compliant baseplates during DED. Despite variations between predictions and measurements, the general trends agree. It also revealed that initial flatness errors in baseplates significantly affect its deviation during deposition. Predictions indicate that compliant features significantly affect the thermal distribution as well as the evolution of flatness deviation in the baseplate during deposition. Notably, one design exhibited a reduction in distortion during cooling, following its initial increase during deposition. FE predictions show a maximum reduction of 60.9% and 38.8% in net flatness deviation for the C- and T-parts, respectively. The performance of compliant baseplates is found to be governed by both its the thermal and mechanical characteristics, which are crucial factors to be considered during design. Finally, the residual strain at the build-baseplate interface has been significantly reduced in the presence of complaint features.

title: Uncovering microstructure evolution in Fe-6.5Si alloy during powder bed fusion electron beam melting: A multiphysics simulation study
abstract: Here, we uncover the microstructure evolution in Fe-6.5Si (wt%) during powder bed fusion electron beam melting using a virtual prototyping framework that integrates the discrete element method for powder-bed generation, computational thermal–fluid dynamics with free-surface melt flow, and a coupled cellular automaton–finite element model incorporating heterogeneous and epitaxial nucleation. Multi-track and multilayer melting were investigated at a constant linear energy of 2.0 J/mm by varying scan speed (200–1000 mm/s) and line offset (50–150 μm). Experiments and simulations consistently showed that reduced line offset enhances heat accumulation, preferentially deepening the melt pool through suppressed lateral heat dissipation and evaporation-driven recoil effects, which broadens the distribution of solidification direction ( SD ) and promotes competitive grain growth. Increasing line offset stabilizes SD toward the build direction but increases the mean undercooling, activating heterogeneous nucleation and reducing columnar aspect ratio. In multilayer melting, microstructure selection could not be explained by SD or mean undercooling alone. Instead, heterogeneous nucleation was governed by the residence time of cells in the supercooled state. Despite the higher undercooling observed at a scan speed of 1000 mm/s, the short and spatially uniform solidification time effectively suppressed new grain formation, enabling sustained epitaxial growth and resulting in the highest texture index and a single-crystal-like microstructure. Based on these findings, processing guidelines for achieving a single-crystal-like microstructure are proposed: (i) suppress heterogeneous nucleation by limiting the effective undercooling, (ii) form a thin melt pool to align the SD with the build direction, and (iii) minimize the solidification time by promoting rapid solid–liquid interface migration.

Fabrication of low-porosity and low-resistance microscale copper structures via autocatalytic plating of laser-printed precursors
From remelting cycles to sustained melting: Defect and microstructure in laser powder bed fusion of AA6061 with modulated laser
abstract: To mitigate defects and control microstructure in additively manufactured AA6061 via laser powder bed fusion, this study systematically investigates modulated laser processing by varying frequency and duty cycle and correlates the resulting thermal histories with melt–pool behavior, defects, microstructure, and mechanical properties. Across 10–50 kHz and 50–75% duty cycle with laser power of 450–550 W, experiments combined with transient melt–pool simulations reveal two distinct melting regimes. In a remelting–cycle regime (lower duty cycle and/or lower frequency), periodic melt/solidification events produce shallower melt pools with multiple melt pool boundaries within a single track; increasing frequency at low duty cycle further increases boundary multiplicity. This regime reduces cracking and refines grains/subgrains with weaker textures. In a sustained–melting regime (higher duty cycle and frequency), the melt pool remains above the liquidus, yielding deeper pools with a single boundary per track (continuous–laser–like behavior), which suppresses lack–of–fusion porosity but coarsens the microstructure, strengthens texture, and lowers the high–angle grain boundary fraction by ~30% relative to the remelting–cycle regime. The optimal condition achieves ~0.3% porosity with ~0.1% crack density. In the as–built state, the remelting–cycle regime yields the highest mean hardness (~71 HV) and yield strength (~108 MPa), while precipitation and elemental segregation trends remain broadly comparable across modulated–laser and continuous–laser conditions. Post–build T6 heat treatment largely preserves grain/subgrain differences but homogenizes precipitate distributions and phase constituents, generally increasing mean hardness and yield strength up to 110-120 HV and 230-278 MPa, respectively. Overall, this study uncovers how the frequency–duty cycle control of remelting cycles governs defect formation and microstructure evolution, enabling practical parameter selection to improve AA6061 printability and performance.

title: A computational modeling framework for polymer melt flow dynamics in material extrusion systems
abstract: We present a computational fluid dynamics framework for simulating polymer melt flow through the hot-end of material extrusion systems with focus on Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) systems. The framework incorporates hybrid constitutive equations with solid-like behavior upstream, and shear-thinning, temperature-dependent melt rheology downstream of the melting interface, ensuring a smooth transition around the glass transition temperature. This approach offers a physically consistent treatment of the solid-to-melt transition using only material properties, without relying on empirical fitting parameters. Additionally, the thermal boundary conditions at the walls of the liquefier are derived from energy conservation principles, considering thermal resistance at the polymer-wall interface and eliminating the need for fitting parameters to match experimental data. Furthermore, we consider the heat penetration towards the heat sink section of the hot-end, which influences the inlet temperature in the computational domain. As well, the momentum boundary condition is set as a combination of slip and no-slip walls before and after the melt front to treat the air gap at the entrance of the filament to the hot end. These physically-based assumptions yield numerical results that align well with experimental data. We validate the simulations by comparing their results with published experimental feeding force measurements for three polymer materials: high-impact polystyrene (HIPS), polylactic acid (PLA), and acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS). The simulations accurately predict the feeding force magnitude and capture the transition from stable to unstable extrusion behavior observed at high feed rates.

title: A new strategy for spatter mitigation in L-PBF with application in direct manufacturing on multimaterial substrates
abstract: Spatter ejections in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF) are recognized among the main drivers of process instability and defect formation. Their occurrence and dynamics are strongly affected by local melting conditions, as insufficient heat dissipation and variations in the thermal regime can trigger intense and localized spattering phenomena. Such conditions can be exacerbated in multi-material L-PBF, where variations in the composition of surrounding and underneath material may alter the heat dissipation, as well as in emerging applications involving direct manufacturing on pre-existing substrates with diminished heat transfer compared to conventional baseplates. Despite extensive studies on spatter formation in L-PBF, their behavior under such challenging conditions remains poorly explored, and effective mitigation strategies are still lacking. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a new strategy based on local pre-sintering to reduce spatter ejections in L-PBF with minimal increase in production time. The effectiveness of the method is assessed under a particularly challenging and novel scenario, in which L-PBF is used to directly manufacture cooling structures on electronic substrates composed of thin layers of copper and ceramic. The limited heat dissipation associated with this configuration exacerbates intense spattering and localized heat accumulation. The study demonstrates that the proposed approach effectively stabilizes both phenomena, enabling the industrial development of L-PBF on electronic substrates. The generality of the method, however, allows it to be extended to applications where material transitions and complex thermal interactions govern spatter formation.

title: Transient interfacial melting promotes bonding in cold spray additive manufacturing of dissimilar metals
abstract: Understanding supersonic impact-induced bonding between dissimilar metals is important for advancing solid-state multi-material manufacturing. While established bonding mechanisms are typically based on plasticity-related indices and are defined for materials with similar properties, here we uncover a hidden dimension of thermo-dynamic mechanisms driving impact-induced bonding of mismatched metals. Atomic-scale simulations reveal transient melting initiating at the substrate surface upon impact and rapidly propagating across the interface. STEM-EDX analysis identifies an oxygen-rich interfacial layer (∼17–20 nm), more than twice as thick as the native oxide, with SAED confirming new oxide formation. Band-shaped segregations within the Impact-Affected Zone (IAZ), ultrafine subgrains (∼100 nm), and alloy-enriched precipitates adjacent to the IAZ are also observed. Together with the simulation results, these features are consistent with transient interfacial melting followed by rapid re-solidification. These findings highlight melting, rapid re-solidification, and the resulting microstructural transitions as significant contributors to metallurgical bonding in mismatched metallic systems, representing a thermodynamic pathway distinct from the widely accepted plasticity-based mechanisms. These insights advance the understanding of dissimilar-material joining and support the development of next-generation additive manufacturing technologies.

In-situ neutron diffraction study on the relationship between mechanical response and post-build Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) of EB-PBF 316 L stainless steel
abstract: Hot Isostatic Press (HIP) post-processing is widely employed to enhance the performance of additive manufacturing components. However, its impact on 316L Electron Beam Powder Bed Fusion (EB-PBF) materials remains unexplored. This study investigated the effects of HIP temperature on 316L EB-PBF materials compared to as-built (AB) and powder metallurgy (PM) counterparts. In-situ neutron diffraction during tensile testing, performed with the loading direction parallel to the build direction, along with microstructural analysis, was conducted to assess the influence of HIP temperature on dislocation evolution, stress distribution, and the resulting mechanical behavior during deformation. The results revealed variations among the different product states. Differences in microstructural features, including grain size, twinning, lattice strain, and dislocation density, were observed and linked to the mechanical response. The PM product exhibited higher stiffness (193 GPa) than the AB EB-PBF product (120 GPa) while showing similar flow strength. HIP treatment significantly influenced the stress-strain behavior of EB-PBF products, affecting dislocation density and stress distribution amongst various grain orientations. These findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of EB-PBF products subjected to HIP post-processing and highlight the differences compared to PM products.

title: Hybrid FEM-multitask neural network approach for processing map prediction in LPBF of novel AlFeCrX alloys
abstract: The development of reliable predictive models for additive manufacturing (AM) remains challenging due to the limited availability of experimental data and the high costs associated with the process, particularly when working with novel alloy systems. In this study, we propose a hybrid modeling approach, that integrates finite element modeling (FEM) with artificial neural networks (ANNs) and transfer learning (TL), to predict melt pool size and defect types, specifically lack-of-fusion and keyhole porosity, and to generate processing maps for three novel aluminum alloys (AlFeCrSi, AlFeCrTi, and AlFeCrSiTi) designed for Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF). To achieve this, first, a melt pool database was generated through FEM simulations incorporating laser and material parameters. This database, containing 1386 melt pools, was trained on melt pool data to generate an initial ANN model. Subsequently, by transfer learning (TL-ANN), the model was fine-tuned using experimental measurements from 108 additively manufactured samples corresponding to three new Al-based alloys. By leveraging finite element simulation data, the TL-ANN model achieved high predictive accuracy with reduced experimental input, providing a practical framework for efficient process optimization and defect mitigation in LPBF of new materials. While the trained source model is transferable to other aluminum alloys with limited experimental datasets, the proposed hybrid methodology is broadly applicable to different metallic materials, enabling the rapid and cost-efficient generation of processing maps. Additionally, the processing maps predicting defect-type regions indicate the existence of an upper laser power threshold beyond which the formation of fully dense material becomes unlikely.

title: In situ monitoring of lunar regolith in PBF-LB: analyzing thermal history and densification mechanisms for improving part quality

One-shot learning of heat equation for scan-path-agnostic process modeling of directed energy deposition
abstract: In directed energy deposition processes, the thermal history determines the quality of the manufactured part, affecting material properties, dimensional tolerances, and potential failure. Accurate finite element-based thermal process simulations help determine the best scan strategy but can be computationally expensive to perform multiple times. Data-driven models can be fast approximators but need many simulations for a dataset. This work proposes a one-shot deep learning method by training a neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) model using only one process simulation. The neural ODE model uses only features identified in the governing transient spatial heat equation and ODE solvers to integrate the results in time. Leave-all-but-one-out cross-validation confirms one simulation is sufficient to generalize well across all cases with different scan strategies, regardless of the training simulation. This simple model with one sample has an R 2 accuracy around 0.9 for the best fold and evaluates the part history faster than real-time and 20x faster than the finite element-based simulation. The method is well suited for rapidly exploring different scan paths to mitigate local heat buildup in a given part geometry.

title: Rheological behavior of the cementitious material: From rheometer to extrusion process of 3D concrete printing
Model-based waveform optimization for frequency-robust electrohydrodynamic jet printing
abstract: Electrohydrodynamic (EHD) jet printing is a high-resolution material jetting process in which droplets are selectively deposited to fabricate microscale functional devices for applications such as printed electronics and sensors. A core principle of material jetting techniques is the repetitive and consistent nature of the process, in which the meniscus advances toward the substrate during droplet ejection and recedes toward the nozzle under constant bias voltage at predictable rates and distances. However, at elevated jetting frequencies, the available relaxation time between pulses becomes comparable to the meniscus recovery dynamics, which leads to significant variability in the deposited volume per pulse and introduces further process complexities. This work presents a model-based waveform design approach that shapes the bias voltage during the relaxation phase to promote consistent meniscus recovery across a wide range of jetting frequencies. By leveraging a physics-based model of the ink meniscus, the voltage waveform is optimized offline to guide the meniscus to a reference pre-pulse state. Experimental results show that the optimized waveform maintains droplet diameters within 5% of the 38 µm target over jetting frequencies of 10-300 Hz, whereas a traditional fixed-bias waveform exhibits a diameter increase of nearly 28% across the same frequency range. These results indicate that dynamic baseline voltages can improve droplet consistency and stability in EHD jet printing across a range of operating conditions.

Predictive and numerical modelling of discolouration and its correlation with mechanical and dimensional properties of PBF-LB/P PA11 parts
abstract: Laser beam powder bed fusion of polymers (PBF-LB/P) with polyamide 11 (PA11) enables structural components while limiting negative environmental impact. However, the material remains sensitive, to not yet fully understood, thermal history effects, pronounced as visible discoloration and variability in mechanical performance. This work quantifies the synergistic effect of laser power and part placement in the build chamber on color change, mechanical properties, and dimensional response of PA11 PBF-LB/P parts, and develops predictive tools to guide pre-build decisions. A structured experimental design varied laser power, build height, and lateral position. For each specimen, we measured CIELAB color coordinates, ultimate tensile strength (UTS), elongation at break (EAB), and dimensional deviations. We then built two complementary predictors: (i) a regression-based response surface across the process window and (ii) a chamber-scale thermo-kinetic simulation that computes transient temperatures and maps discoloration using an Arrhenius-type degradation law. Laser power was the primary driver of all responses, while chamber position introduced secondary but consistent effects that reflected non-uniform thermal exposure; discoloration and shrinkage were greatest toward the chamber interior. A simple color-based degradation metric combining lightness and yellowness showed the strongest association with UTS and EAB, providing a practical indicator of thermal ageing. The simulation captured the spatial pattern of degradation both in the designed experiment and for a large industrial impeller. Together, these data-driven and physics-based approaches enable prediction and mitigation of discoloration and associated material degradation, supporting robust pre-build parameter selection and process optimization.

title: Synthesis of lattice tiles using dualities of space filling polyhedra
Spot melting of ultra-dense tungsten via electron beam powder bed fusion: A reproducible fabrication strategy
abstract: ABSTRACT Tungsten is crucial for extreme-environment applications; however, its fabrication by additive manufacturing is challenging due to its high melting temperature, ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, oxygen sensitivity, steep thermal gradients, and strong susceptibility to cracking. In this work, a spot-melting strategy is introduced using electron beam powder bed fusion (E-PBF) to enable repeatable fabrication of highly dense tungsten with crack-free microstructures in the sectioned specimens. The approach integrates a Defocused-Focused-Defocused (DFD) spot sequence with island-based segmentation and stochastic spot jumping to minimize steep thermal gradients and mitigate solidification cracking, under high pre-heating temperatures (~1200 °C) and vacuum conditions. Using this strategy, two builds of nine cuboids each, 18 in total, were fabricated with consistently ultra-high density (~99.9304 ± 0.0152% on average), with representative specimens exhibiting crack-free microstructures, demonstrating exceptional process stability and reproducibility. Microstructural characterization reveals coarse columnar grains aligned with the build direction, a strong θ -fiber texture 001 // Z, and a dense network of low-angle subgrain boundaries, indicative of early-stage dynamic recrystallization. Direct observation of the microstructure on the as-solidified top surfaces without conventional metallographic preparation also revealed a strong 001 // Z texture, while cross-sectional characterization confirmed its persistence throughout the build thickness, indicating that surface measurements can be representative of the bulk material. Mechanical testing demonstrates that E-PBF spot-melted tungsten achieves a room-temperature ultimate compressive strength of ~1.75 GPa with substantial inelastic strain, comparable to wrought tungsten and exceeding laser powder bed fusion counterparts. At elevated temperatures (800 – 1400 °C), compressive flow stresses remain below the deformation-processed wrought-rod baseline while exhibiting continued strain hardening up to ε inel ≈ 0.3 . These results establish spot melting in E-PBF as a reproducible pathway for fabricating brittle refractory metals.

title: Support-free 4D printing of self-sensing shape-memory piezoelectric multifunctional structures via frontal polymerization
abstract: The integration of structural programmability and self-sensing capability in additively manufactured materials remains a significant challenge, particularly for free-standing geometries fabricated without external support. Here, we report a support-free 4D printing strategy enabled by frontal ring-opening metathesis polymerization to fabricate self-sensing shape-memory piezoelectric multifunctional structures. By incorporating BaTiO3 (BT) nanoparticles into a dicyclopentadiene-based shape memory polymer matrix, we establish a composite system that simultaneously exhibits programmable shape recovery and electromechanical transduction. The rapid, self-propagating curing front allows the direct writing of free-standing geometries in air, eliminating the need for sacrificial supports while maintaining structural fidelity. The resulting composites demonstrate a high shape recovery ratio (~93%) and stable piezoelectric output under cyclic deformation over 1,000 loading cycles, with an optimized BT content of 30 wt%. Importantly, the printed structures enable real-time electrical signal generation during both externally applied mechanical loading and intrinsic shape recovery processes, highlighting their capability as self-sensing systems. This work establishes a versatile platform for the fabrication of architected multifunctional materials, where structural reconfiguration and sensing are intrinsically coupled.

title: In-process alignment of dual-laser powder bed fusion scanfields using off-axis bed imaging
A multi-GPU-centric finite element multiphysics modeling framework for vat photopolymerization
