Porosity control during directed energy deposition additive manufacturing through La2O3 particle additions
abstract: Porosity in laser powder-based directed energy deposition (DED) additive manufactured alloy components may compromise mechanical performance. This study demonstrates how La2O3 particles blended with gas atomised RR1000 Ni-based superalloy powder affect pore evolution, reducing the occurrence of porosity, especially large pores. Using correlative in situ high-speed synchrotron X-ray and infrared imaging coupled with multiphysics modelling, we reveal the underlying melt flow and pore evolution behaviour with and without La2O3 additions. A 0.2 wt.% La2O3 particulate addition produces a pore-lean build with notably fewer large pores. We propose this occurs through two mechanisms involving La2O3 on the surface altering thermo-fluid conditions within the melt pool: (1) a reduction of melt pool surface tension gradient and hence Marangoni flow, and (2) an increased melt pool absorptivity. Additionally, La2O3 enhances powder capture efficiency and promotes the formation of a predominantly equiaxed, fine-grained microstructure.

title: Autocatalytic gelation-driven 3D printing of hybrid aerogels with high strength and thermal insulation
abstract: Leveraging the unique capability of customizing complex architectures, 3D-printed aerogels have shown significant potential for applications in various fields, including microelectronic thermal management, aerospace thermal protection, highly efficient electromagnetic interference shielding, next-generation energy storage devices, and biomedical engineering. Nevertheless, the practical application of these materials is currently hindered by critical challenges such as printing ink instability, insufficient thermal insulation performance, and low mechanical strength. To address these challenges, this study reports a novel direct ink writing 3D printing strategy driven by the autocatalytic gelation mechanism of bis[3-(trimethoxysilyl)propyl]amine, successfully fabricating hybrid aerogels that combine robust mechanical strength with highly efficient thermal insulation. Specifically, this strategy utilizes an ethanol–water bath as an instant coagulation medium, which offers the dual advantages of a facile fabrication process and excellent long-term storage stability for the precursor inks. The as-prepared hybrid aerogels exhibit exceptional low-density and high-strength characteristics, achieving a remarkable compressive strength of up to 9.19 MPa. Furthermore, the highly interconnected internal nanoporous network endows the material with an exceptionally low thermal conductivity of 0.025 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹, demonstrating excellent thermal insulation capabilities. Consequently, this study provides an effective strategy for the design and development of high-performance, customizable thermal management materials.

title: Novel beam scanning optimisation in laser cladding by solving the inverse problem of heat placement
abstract: Additive manufacturing by laser cladding has gained popularity in recent years but optimising the outcomes (e.g. microstructure) remains a challenge due to the difficulty of heat placement control. To address this, research has been conducted to generate a more uniform temperature distribution to seek hinger mechanical properties by beam oscillation strategies. However, these approaches need to determine the optimal conditions from a significant number of parameter combinations, which requires extensive iterative trials. Moreover, fixed parameters and constant motion paths still generate localised laser energy concentrations. In this work we proposed a novel laser beam scanning optimisation approach, whereby the heat placement can be controlled by tuning the laser beam configuration through solving the inverse problem. Unlike conventional approaches, it directly derives optimised parameter patterns from a target temperature distribution, eliminating the need for iterative simulations and experiments. A speed-controlled beam path strategy is implemented to realise a uniform target temperature on the wire feeding surface during stainless steel 316L deposition. Thermal analysis proved that the optimised system achieved the uniform temperature distribution on the cladding surface, within the target temperature on the cladding surface for ensuring a thermally and microstructurally stable deposition. Experimental characteristics also confirmed that suppressing temperature fluctuations and the effectively restriction of grain coarsening and precipitation, leading to a substantially finer and more homogeneous grain structure compared to the conventional linear scan. This research also shows potential for future application of other laser heat placement control processes such as selective laser melting or laser heat treatments.

title: Stress evolution during multilayer stacking of elastoviscoplastic materials in extrusion-based additive manufacturing
Binder jetting-inspired powder bed printing as a solvent‑minimized manufacturing route for lithium‑ion battery electrodes
Improving path fidelity at speed in melt electrowriting
abstract: Melt electrowriting (MEW) delivers unrivaled micron-scale fiber placement precision among extrusion-based additive manufacturing methods, yet its speed is fundamentally limited by jet lag or offset between nozzle motion and polymer jet landing induced by the electric field-driven drawing process. Maintaining path fidelity typically requires operating near the critical translation speed to keep the jet nearly vertical, which preserves accuracy but constrains throughput. Here, we present a geometric path-planning strategy that overcomes this longstanding speed-fidelity trade-off. Inspired by drag knife cutting systems, which correct for a trailing blade’s offset to accurately track sharp contours, we introduced a predictive geometric code correction method that compensates for MEW jet lag. This approach enables high-speed printing while preserving precise fiber placement. Using this method, we demonstrated up to a threefold increase in printing speed with sustained high fidelity in serpentine and triangular geometries. While restraints remain for sharp corners at elevated speeds, stemming from current modeling constraints such as the absence of acceleration, our results indicate that hardware capable of faster directional changes will mitigate this limit. Overall, this drag knife-inspired correction framework enables stable jet behavior and improves path fidelity during MEW printing at higher speeds that would otherwise exhibit substantial lag-induced deviations. This enhances MEW throughput and supports the fabrication of commonly used MEW micro-architected designs at elevated printing speeds. Importantly, this controller-agnostic strategy operates at the command level and therefore has the potential to be integrated into additive manufacturing platforms that utilize comparable motion-control architectures without hardware modifications.

title: From coupons to full-scale components: Predicting fracture in complex Ti-6Al-4V brackets
Deformation mechanisms and strain partitioning in WE43 Mg alloy with heterogeneous microstructure processed by additive friction stir deposition
abstract: A WE43 Mg alloy with heterogeneous microstructure, featuring grain sizes ranging from 25 μm to 1 μm arranged in alternating bands, was manufactured via solid-state additive friction stir deposition technique. The alloy exhibits a favourable strength-ductility balance in tension, with a yield strength of 201 ± 13 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 270 ± 5 MPa, and a uniform elongation of 17.1 ± 2.0%, outperforming many additively manufactured Mg alloys reported to date. The dominant deformation mechanisms were ascertained at different length scales, and involve basal slip, extension twinning, and limited non-basal slip, which operates across all grain size populations, but their relative activities are sensitive to grain size. The gradual yielding of grains with different sizes—from coarse to fine—induces pronounced strain partitioning and dislocation accumulation at their interfaces. This synergistic interaction sustains strain hardening during deformation and effectively alleviates the conventional strength-ductility trade-off. These findings provide multiscale insights into the deformation behaviour and strain-distribution mechanisms of heterogeneous Mg alloys processed by additive manufacturing.

title: Micro-architected Metallic Metamaterial Composites by Data-driven Generative Design and Binder Jetting Additive Manufacturing
abstract: This study describes a novel design and manufacturing approach for an optimized two-phase aluminum matrix, silicon carbide-reinforced cellular metamaterial composite with a low coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). The design was generated with Bayesian optimization to obtain a periodic cellular pattern with the minimum coefficient of thermal expansion. The manufacturing was achieved via binder jetting additive manufacturing, followed by liquid aluminum infiltration. The barrier coating layer of Si-SiO 2 and the cooling rate after infiltration were found to be critical for suppressing the reaction between the two phases and maintaining the silicon carbide phase. A comparable study found that a proactive cooling rate as high as 20 °C/min could maintain a phase fraction of silicon carbide up to 12 wt.% in the manufactured composite, leading to minimized CTE values in multiple cycles of a single sample and repeatable values across various samples. The thermal cycling test validated the performance of the manufactured composite at high temperatures up to 350 °C. This study explored the design-manufacturing-test route for a novel metallic metamaterial composite, opening a wide research direction for advanced materials in harsh environments.

title: EBSD-based misorientation metrics for plastic strain quantification in laser additive manufacturing alloys
Suppression of powder spattering in powder bed fusion with core-ring laser beam
abstract: Powder spattering and denudation are critical issues in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) processes, both of which contribute to the formation of defects in the fabricated parts. Recent experimental studies have demonstrated that non-Gaussian laser beam profiles can significantly alter powder spattering and denudation behavior. However, the fundamental laser/gas-powder interactions governing these phenomena remain insufficiently understood. In this study, a combination of experimental and numerical approaches is employed to investigate the use of a core-ring beam configuration comprising a Gaussian core beam and an auxiliary ring-shaped beam. A range of core-to-ring power ratios, with varying total laser powers, is explored under a constant scanning speed of 0.4 m/s, using Ti-6Al-4V powder/substrate in an Argon environment. The analysis focuses on the quasi-steady-state stage, examining the effects of core/ring laser power ratios. Powder behavior was observed experimentally via high-speed imaging, while a fully coupled three-dimensional multiphysics model was employed to simulate vapor plume dynamics, entrained gas flow, and powder motion. Among those configurations, the case with 70 W applied to both the core and the ring beams demonstrates the most pronounced spattering suppression. The underlying mechanisms responsible for this effect are elucidated through detailed simulation analyses. These findings highlight the potential of auxiliary laser beam modulation as an effective strategy for reducing powder spattering and thereby improving part quality in LPBF.

title: Data-driven prediction of nominal composition of a steel to copper multi material using hyperspectral in-situ monitoring of the Directed Energy Deposition process
abstract: Laser-based Directed Energy Deposition (DED-LB) enables the fabrication of multi-material and compositionally graded metallic components. Yet, ensuring accurate local composition during printing remains a major challenge, especially critical for systems with strongly dissimilar physical and thermo-physical properties. In this study, a hyperspectral in-situ monitoring approach is proposed to detect and quantify compositional variations during the DED-LB fabrication of 316L to CuCr 1 Zr multi-material structures. Hyperspectral imaging captures the spatially resolved spectral emission of the melt pool, providing a high-dimensional representation of its thermal and radiative state that is sensitive to changes in material composition. A data-driven model based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) is trained to correlate hyperspectral signatures with the local compositional ratio under varying processing conditions, enabling real-time classification of compositional states during deposition. The proposed method demonstrates high accuracy in identifying compositional transitions and detecting deviations from the designed gradient, even in the presence of melt pool instabilities inherent to the Fe–Cu system. Post-process characterization confirms a strong agreement between hyperspectral predictions and measured elemental composition. These results highlight the potential of hyperspectral in-situ monitoring and CNN classification as a powerful tool for real-time composition sensing and closed-loop control in multi-material DED-LB, paving the way toward more reliable fabrication of functionally graded metallic components.

title: Anisotropic behavior of cable-reinforced 3D-printed concrete: Experimental investigation and deep learning-based stress field prediction
Multiwavelength considerations in two-photon lithography using carbon quantum dot initiators
Atmosphere-controlled post-curing extends the service life of vat-photopolymerized soft tooling for injection molding
abstract: ABSTRACT Vat photopolymerization enables rapid fabrication of soft tooling for injection molding (IM), but photopolymer inserts often fail too quickly for stable production. Although suppressing oxygen inhibition is an established method, how post-curing atmosphere affects through-thickness gradients and dimensional stabilization in VPP for tooling remains unclear. Using a clear high-temperature photopolymer, we show that atmosphere-controlled post-curing strongly influences insert lifetime. Relative to ambient post-curing, nitrogen-assisted post-curing increased life at both industrial and laboratory IM systems and, critically, extended it enough for the molding process to pass through an initial conditioning stage and reach a stable dimensional regime that ambient-cured inserts never attained. Nitrogen-assisted first-stage post-curing was associated with later visual crack detection in the evaluated inserts. The magnitude of the observed lifetime extension was dependent on the insert geometry and injection-molding process parameters. Cross-sectional nanoindentation and spectroscopy revealed depth-dependent mechanical and conversion gradients through the insert thickness. Under cyclic thermo-mechanical loading both systems evolved, but the nitrogen-cured inserts retained this gradient longer, consistent with slower redistribution of mobile residual species and greater resistance to structural homogenization. Across seven independent insert trials spanning laboratory- and industrial-scale process windows, the pooled descriptive crack-initiation life, N i , was 827±123 cycles for the nitrogen-cured inserts (n=3), compared with 193±55 cycles for the ambient-cured inserts (n=4). These results further motivate rethinking IM process windows for soft tooling: insert lifetime, rather than cycle time, governs the suitability of photopolymer tooling for IM.

title: Local pore prediction in laser powder bed fusion of metals using dual off-axis photodiode monitoring and spatiotemporal deep learning
abstract: Accurate pore identification and localization remain major challenges in laser powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M). This study presents an X-ray computed tomography (XCT)-labelled framework for local pore detection using dual off-axis photodiode signals. Each build layer was divided into patches, and each target patch was stacked with spatially corresponding patches from adjacent layers to form a sampling cuboid. These cuboids were registered to XCT-derived labels. DualFusionNet combines 3D-CNN and ConvLSTM encoders: the 3D-CNN extracts localized volumetric correlations across tracks and layers, whereas the ConvLSTM preserves layer order to model thermal evolution associated with successive melting and remelting events. Trained and tested on M789 maraging steel, the model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.93. Probability-of-detection (POD) analysis yielded a corrected a 90 of 96 µm, where a 90 denotes the spherical equivalent diameter at which the fitted POD curve reaches 90%. Ablation studies confirmed that encoder diversity and fusion of the two photodiode channels improved pore prediction performance. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping revealed distinct yet partially overlapping salient regions within the sampling cuboid, consistent with the encoders’ complementary roles in capturing spatial-interlayer structure and sequential dependencies. DualFusionNet required 0.25 ms per patch for inference and completed end-to-end processing of a representative 784-patch layer in 5.8 s, including data loading and preprocessing. This fits within the nominal 6 s recoating interval, supporting near-real-time layerwise prediction. DualFusionNet achieved an AUROC of 0.91 and 85.0% recall on an additional 9 × 9 × 12 mm³ specimen produced using different process parameters (laser power: 440 to 410 W; scan speed: 820 to 750 mm/s; hatch spacing: 97 to 95 µm; and layer rotation: 67° to 90°). Recall reached 91.9% for pores larger than the established 96 µm detection size, demonstrating within-platform transfer under moderate process variations. Extension to substantially different process windows, machines, or materials requires further validation and may necessitate sensor recalibration, adjustment of the sampling-cuboid dimensions, and model fine-tuning or retraining. These results establish a practical route toward in-situ local pore detection and layerwise decision support in PBF-LB/M tooling applications, providing a foundation for future corrective control.

title: Systematic analysis of penalty-optimised illumination design for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing via the extendable framework TVAM AID using the Core Imaging Library
abstract: Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing (TVAM) is a novel manufacturing method that allows for the fast creation of objects of complex geometry in layerless fashion. The process is based on the solidification of photopolymer that occurs when a sufficient threshold dose of light-energy is absorbed. In order to create complex shapes, an illumination plan must be designed to force solidification in some desired areas while leaving other regions liquid. Determining an illumination plan can be considered as an optimisation problem where a variety of objective functionals (penalties) can be used. This work presents a systematic evaluation of a selection of penalty functions and their impact on selected printing metrics; linking the shape of penalty functions to ranges of light-energy dose levels in in-part regions that should be printed and out-of-part regions that should remain liquid. Further, the threshold parameters that are typically used to demarcate minimum light-energy for in-part regions and maximum light-energy for out-of-part regions are investigated systematically as design parameters to characterise their influence on illumination plan quality. This enables the characterisation of their effects on some selected dose field metrics as well as informed selection for default values within the adopted binary material model. This work is underpinned by a reproducible and extensible framework, TVAM Adaptive Illumination Design (TVAM AID), which makes use of the open-source Core Imaging Library (CIL) that is designed for tomographic imaging with an emphasis on reconstruction. The foundation of TVAM AID which is presented here can hence be easily enhanced by existing functionality in CIL thus lowering the barrier to entry and encouraging use of strategies that already exist for reconstruction optimisation.

Mechanics of corners in material extrusion additive manufacturing
abstract: Corners are among the most common yet least understood features in material extrusion additive manufacturing (MEX AM). They are present in almost all toolpaths, especially lattices and infills, impacting structural integrity and shear flow, especially for fibre reinforced composites. However, corners have rarely been studied as microstructure-governing mechanical entities. This is the first microstructure-mechanics study for 3D‑printed corners, revealing how corner geometries dynamically affect crack growth and direction, stress concentration, cyclic degradation, and fibre kinematics. Multi-layer single-filament corners with varied angles were 3D printed and tested. For monotonic tensile, force reduction and brittle-to-flexible transition with turn angles were found across multiple materials. For short-fibre composites, microstructural evolution of corners was identified with dynamic crack and fibre behaviours. Displacement-controlled cyclic tensile tests showed displacement dependency on self-stiffening and degradation of force, energy dissipation and increase of stiffness. The displacement-controlled cyclic tension also reveals several competing mechanisms for fibre-reinforced composites (fibre re-orientation and strain-hardening versus damage accumulation). The force-controlled cyclic tension showed a peak displacement growth and rapid energy dissipation over cycles. Next, compared to angular corners, rounded corners demonstrate that curvature effectively suppressed stress concentration and improved strength (>7-fold for normalised force), supported by a case study of zigzag lattices with rounded corners. This study transforms corners in MEX AM from incidental geometry into primary microstructural features that govern performance of printed parts, revealing how corner‑induced microstructures could affect load transfer, deformation modes, failure evolution, and fatigue. The findings provide an insight of corner‑aware toolpath strategies that enhance structural integrity and mitigate mechanical weakness or stress concentration in MEX AM.

title: Decoupled in situ auxiliary-laser surface heating for low-stress laser powder bed fusion
Additively manufactured ceramic façades for biodiversity and climatic performance integration: A full-scale case study
abstract: This paper presents a multiscale design-to-production workflow for additively manufactured ceramic façade elements that integrate biodiversity-supporting nesting sites and climate-responsive surface geometries, while remaining compatible with standard ventilated façade substructures. The research combines (i) material and process optimisation for extrusion-based clay 3D-printing, (ii) fabrication-aware computational design from building scale to printing path scale, and (iii) standards-referenced mechanical assessment.Material development focused on mitigating shrinkage-induced deformation and cracking by optimising clay–grog–water–additive ratios and controlling drying conditions. An optimised clay mixture, in combination with a material-informed printing-path strategy, reduced the root mean square (RMS) deviation of the 3D-printed elements to up to 1.56 mm (up to 49%) compared to elements with unoptimised mixtures and printing paths. Deformation was quantified using 3D scanning and target-actual deviation analysis, with particular attention to rear-surface planarity to ensure mounting-system fit. Controlled high-humidity drying reduced cracking rates to below 10% in optimised geometries.Mechanical performance was evaluated using an adapted three-point bending test methodology based on DIN EN 14411 and DIN EN ISO 10545-4. In the optimised material-process configuration used for the prototype, specimens achieved average modulus-of-rupture values of 11 N/mm² parallel to print layers (and up to ~25 N/mm² perpendicular), primarily complying with façade-tile requirements (≥8 N/mm²), with breaking loads above the 600 N threshold. The workflow was verified through the design and production of a 12 m² façade installation in Munich, integrating species-specific nesting cavities and site-specific self-shading elements, built into a standard ventilated façade system. First climate measurements showed a surface temperature reduction of up to 16 °C compared to an unventilated reference façade. The prototype provides a long-term testbed for future ecological occupancy monitoring and further microclimatic performance assessment under real-world conditions

title: Atomic faulting enables superior strength and plasticity in a Ni-rich medium-entropy superalloy
Effect of residual stresses on fatigue crack growth for laser powder bed fusion fabricated AlSi10Mg
abstract: Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) produces complex thermal gradients during processing, leading to residual stress formation that can affect fatigue performance. When fabricating AlSi10Mg components via LPBF, there are many process parameter combinations that give similar high-density parts; however, little consideration is often given to selecting parameters that minimize residual stresses and their subsequent effects on the fatigue behavior. This study investigated the effects of residual stresses on fatigue crack growth rates in LPBF fabricated AlSi10Mg using two sets of LPBF process parameters known to give high and low residual stresses. Fatigue crack growth experiments were conducted using compact tension samples under a decreasing applied stress intensity factor range at a 0.1 load ratio, measuring both the Paris law and the near-threshold regime. Residual stresses were measured by neutron diffraction, slitting-compliance, and an on-line compliance method during fatigue crack growth. Compressive residual stresses in the center of the “high stress” as-built specimens gave higher levels of crack closure and higher fatigue thresholds compared to both “low stress” as-built and annealed “stress-free” specimens. When fatigue crack growth rates were corrected for crack closure and superimposed residual stresses at the crack tip, the crack growth data largely collapsed onto a single curve. Different levels of crack closure accounted for most of the residual stress and microstructure related differences in the fatigue crack growth properties of as-built and annealed samples in two orientations. The findings of this study provide guidance for selecting LPBF process parameters to achieve low residual stress and low variability in the fatigue performance of as-built LPBF fabricated AlSi10Mg.

Vision-based control of contact tip to work distance in dot-by-dot WAAM of Al4043
abstract: The dot-by-dot approach in Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing (WAAM) represents a fundamental shift from conventional continuous deposition, enabling the fabrication of complex, lightweight three-dimensional aluminum lattice structures. While this strategy offers superior morphological control, it is highly susceptible to heat accumulation, which triggers a progressive and uncontrolled increase in the Contact Tip to Work Distance (CTWD). In aluminum alloys, the lack of a reliable correlation between electrical arc signals and CTWD complicates real-time height regulation, often leading to process instability and compromised shielding gas effectiveness. To address this challenge, this study proposes a vision-based framework leveraging a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for real-time CTWD sensing, by detecting the wire tip during the discrete cooling intervals between consecutive droplets. The output of the supervised machine learning architecture is subsequently mapped to the CTWD through a linear regression model. Two different control strategies are assessed within this research to regulate the CTWD during the dot-by-dot deposition of Al4043 single struts: a rule-based scheme without inter-droplet waiting times and an adaptive robot motion strategy that dynamically adjusts the vertical step-up based on real-time height estimation. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approaches enable stable deposition of aluminum single struts up to the target height while preserving process stability. In addition, a comprehensive geometrical and mechanical characterization was performed for the different control strategies, allowing their respective advantages and limitations to be identified. Finally, the approach provides a solid basis for future extensions toward more complex, multi-strut assemblies.

title: Top-surface topography and defect formation in laser-based powder bed fusion of Inconel 718: The role of remelting, confinement, and melt pool instabilities
abstract: Surface-tension-driven melt pool instabilities limit productivity in laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), particularly at high scan speeds and low relative beam overlap that reduce remelting and lateral confinement. While beam shaping can mitigate instabilities such as humping, characteristic top-surface patterns, including bulging, waviness, and irregular topographies, remain insufficiently understood. This work systematically investigates the influence of laser power, scan speed, and hatch distance on the top-surface topography and defect formation of IN718 fabricated using Gaussian and ring-shaped beam profiles. ISO 25178 areal surface parameters and a rule-based classification framework are used to construct process maps and identify governing mechanisms. The results show that hatch distance acts as the primary initiator of surface irregularities by controlling remelting and lateral melt pool confinement, whereas scan speed governs the resulting topography and characteristic wavelength. Increasing the hatch distance reduces inter-track overlap and suppresses remelting-induced smoothing, promoting instability-driven surface features. Increasing the scan speed decreases melt pool width and depth while increasing the melt pool length, driving transitions from continuous to discontinuous surface regimes. Flat surfaces are predominantly associated with high relative beam overlap and sufficient remelting, whereas increasingly irregular surface topographies emerge as overlap decreases. Combining small hatch distances with high scan speeds enables theoretical build rate increases exceeding a factor of two compared to state-of-the-art processing while maintaining a flat top-surface. These findings establish a mechanistic framework linking process parameters, lateral melt pool confinement, remelting, and surface topography, providing guidance for productivity-oriented process window design in PBF-LB/M.

Acoustic emission signatures of crack formation in aluminium-based alloys processed by laser powder bed fusion: Embedded representation learning toward real-time in situ detection
abstract: Additive manufacturing (AM) of dense metallic materials faces challenges from defects such as pores and cracks, especially detrimental to structural performance. In situ crack detection is therefore essential for reliable, defect-free manufacturing. We present a semi-supervised machine learning pipeline for in situ crack detection via acoustic emission (AE) monitoring during laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) of AA2024. Three specimens fabricated at different process conditions yielded near-fully dense, crack-dominated, and porosity-dominated microstructures. Post-build X-ray computed tomography, optical microscopy, and EBSD provide ground-truth characterisation of the defect populations and crack formation mechanism. EBSD identifies the likely microstructural origin of the acoustic signal: solidification cracks propagate intergranularly along high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), whose lower density in the dense specimen explains its reduced crack susceptibility. The burst-type AE signal reflects liquid-film rupture at HAGBs and subsequent crack propagation. High-frequency structure-borne AE signals were continuously recorded and analysed via a three-step pipeline: autoencoder-based embedding of AE events, unsupervised clustering for crack identification, and a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) classifier for real-time-capable labelling. Spectrogram-based embeddings yield the most reliable crack-noise separation, and an MLP with only 105 parameters achieves a mean F 1 -score of 0.93 under stratified, class-weighted cross-validation against HDBSCAN-derived labels, compared to 0.19 for a linear baseline. Jointly trained on AA2024 and Al 92 Mn 6 Ce 2 (at%) data, the pipeline separates crack and noise events despite distinct cracking mechanisms, indicating a shared physical crack signature rather than alloy-specific features. The pipeline is lightweight and computationally real-time-capable, supporting a path toward closed-loop PBF-LB/M process control.
